FOR RETAILERS

A meal plan that ends in a basket.

SmartBasket plans meals against a household's nutrition targets and turns them into what actually has to be bought: whole packages, quantities, a total. Planning does not end at a recipe, it ends at a shopping list that maps onto an assortment.

What the app produces

A finished plan is not recipe text. It is a structure a retailer recognises:

  • ingredients combined across all meals rather than listed per dish
  • converted into whole packages with pack sizes, not gram figures
  • an estimated basket total that can be checked against a budget
  • remaining quantities kept in a pantry and credited against later plans

To see it run: the planning demo on the start page does exactly this in the browser, by voice or by typing.

Where an assortment plugs in

Product data sits in its own layer. Today it comes from Open Food Facts — products, pack sizes, nutrition. That layer could be swapped for a retailer's assortment without touching the planning logic. What would help: article identifiers, pack sizes, prices and, where available, availability.

What works today — and what does not

In place

  • planning against calorie and protein targets, for one or two people across several days
  • conversion into whole packages with a cost estimate
  • a pantry that credits leftover quantities
  • voice-guided intake of the request
  • an Android app in development, with the source open to read

Not in place

  • no ordering and no payment
  • no connection to any retailer system
  • no running pilot and no user numbers
  • no loyalty or account integration

This list is here on purpose. A conversation starts better from an honest position than from an announcement.

Why this can be worth a retailer's while

The pantry saves trips, not revenue. Planning before the shop means buying too little less often and throwing away less — the basket becomes more complete and more predictable rather than smaller. On top of that sits an app people open before they shop, which is where the decision about the assortment is actually made.

What I am looking for

I am looking to talk to retailers who want to try this against their own assortment. Concretely useful would be access to assortment and pack data, and a small pilot that can show whether planned shops really do come out more complete.
